title: Mangroves of the Indus delta
text: Along the coast south of Karachi, where the Indus finally meets the Arabian Sea, lies one of the largest arid-climate mangrove forests in the world. Mangroves are trees that tolerate salt water, and in the Indus delta a single species, Avicennia marina, makes up most of the forest. Its roots send small breathing tubes up through the mud, allowing the tree to take in air even when the soil is waterlogged and poor in oxygen. The forest matters far beyond its own boundaries. Its tangled roots slow incoming waves and hold sediment in place, so villages behind a healthy belt of mangroves suffer less damage when storms strike. The sheltered channels between the trees serve as nurseries where young fish and shrimp grow before moving to open water, which makes the forest important to the coastal fishing economy. Mangrove soils also lock away large amounts of carbon, often more per hectare than many inland forests. Yet mangroves depend on a delicate balance. They need fresh water and silt from the river as well as salt water from the sea. When less river water reaches the delta, the water becomes saltier and fewer seedlings survive. For this reason, people who replant mangroves along the Sindh coast pay close attention to whether some fresh water still reaches the mudflats they plant.

stem: The passage is mainly concerned with
options: the value of the Indus delta mangroves and the conditions they need to survive
the growth of the fishing economy in the villages along the coast south of Karachi
the reasons why Avicennia marina is the only tree able to grow in salt water
a comparison of the carbon stored by coastal forests and by mountain forests
explanation: The passage first describes the forest, then its benefits (storm protection, fish nurseries, carbon), and finally its need for both fresh and salt water. Fishing is only one of the benefits mentioned, and the passage never claims Avicennia marina is the only salt-tolerant tree; it says this species makes up most of this forest.

stem: It can be inferred from the passage that a sharp fall in the amount of river water reaching the delta would most likely
options: make the water around the mangroves less salty
increase the amount of silt settling on the mudflats
reduce the number of mangrove seedlings that survive
have little effect, since mangroves tolerate salt water
explanation: The passage states: 'When less river water reaches the delta, the water becomes saltier and fewer seedlings survive.' A sharp fall in river water is the extreme case of this. The last option is tempting because mangroves tolerate salt, but the passage stresses that they also need fresh water and silt, and less river water would mean less silt, not more.

stem: As used in the passage, the word 'delicate' in 'a delicate balance' most nearly means
options: finely detailed
easily disturbed
gently flavoured
rarely noticed
explanation: The sentences that follow show how the balance between fresh and salt water is upset when river flow falls, so 'delicate' here means easily disturbed. 'Finely detailed' and 'gently flavoured' are other senses of delicate (delicate lace, a delicate taste) that do not fit a balance of water.

title: The karez of Balochistan
text: In the dry valleys of Balochistan, farmers have for centuries drawn water from the ground without pumps or engines. Their method, the karez, is a gently sloping tunnel dug into the base of a hillside until it reaches water-bearing gravel. From there the tunnel carries groundwater, by gravity alone, to fields and villages that may lie several kilometres away. A line of vertical shafts, visible on the surface like a row of craters, marks its route; the shafts were used to remove soil during digging and still allow workers to climb down for cleaning. Because the water travels underground, very little of it is lost to evaporation, a great advantage in a region of hot summers and scarce rain. A karez also has a built-in limit: it can deliver only as much water as seeps into it, so it rarely drains an aquifer faster than rain and snowmelt refill it. Maintenance is shared, and families traditionally receive water in turns measured by time. In recent decades, many karezes have dried up. Electric and diesel tube wells, which can pump water from far deeper levels, have lowered the water table in several valleys. As the water table sinks below the tunnels, the old channels simply stop flowing, and the knowledge needed to maintain them begins to fade along with them.

stem: According to the passage, what is the purpose of the vertical shafts along a karez?
options: They lift water to the surface for drinking.
They let sunlight dry out the tunnel walls.
They mark each family's turn to take water.
They gave access for digging and now for cleaning.
explanation: The passage says the shafts 'were used to remove soil during digging and still allow workers to climb down for cleaning.' Water in a karez flows by gravity to the fields, not up the shafts, and families' turns are 'measured by time', not by the shafts.

stem: The author points out that a karez 'can deliver only as much water as seeps into it' mainly in order to
options: show that a karez supplies too little water for farming
explain why a karez seldom exhausts its source of water
suggest that tube wells are a more dependable source
describe the way the tunnels were originally dug
explanation: The same sentence continues: 'so it rarely drains an aquifer faster than rain and snowmelt refill it.' The limit is presented as a strength that protects the water supply. Nothing in the passage says karez water is too little for farming; the tunnels in fact feed fields and villages.

stem: Which of the following can most reasonably be inferred from the passage?
options: A karez can stop flowing without any damage to its tunnel.
Tube wells lose more of their water to evaporation than karezes do.
Karezes failed mainly because families stopped sharing water in turns.
Most of the karezes in Balochistan were dug within recent decades.
explanation: The end of the passage explains that pumping by tube wells lowers the water table, and 'as the water table sinks below the tunnels, the old channels simply stop flowing.' So a sound tunnel can still run dry. The passage never compares evaporation from tube wells, and it blames falling water tables, not the sharing system, for the decline.

title: How vaccines use the body's memory
text: When a virus or bacterium enters the body for the first time, the immune system needs several days to respond fully. Special white blood cells must recognise the invader, multiply and produce antibodies, proteins that attach to the germ and mark it for destruction. During this delay the person may become seriously ill. Once the infection is defeated, however, some of these cells remain in the body as memory cells. If the same germ returns, the memory cells recognise it at once, and the response is so fast and strong that the person often notices nothing at all. A vaccine makes use of this memory without the danger of the disease. It presents the immune system with a harmless version of the germ, or just one of its parts, such as a surface protein. Some vaccines contain killed germs, some contain weakened ones, and newer types give the body's cells instructions to make the protein themselves. In every case the immune system responds as if a real infection were under way and keeps memory cells afterwards. Vaccination also protects people who cannot be vaccinated, such as newborn babies or those with weakened immunity. When most of a community is immune, a germ finds too few hosts to spread, and outbreaks fade before they can reach the most vulnerable.

stem: Which of the following best states the main idea of the passage?
options: The immune system cannot defeat a germ that it has never met before.
Newer vaccines are safer than those made from killed or weakened germs.
Vaccines let the body form memory cells without suffering the disease.
Antibodies destroy germs directly inside the body's white blood cells.
explanation: The passage explains immune memory and then states that 'a vaccine makes use of this memory without the danger of the disease.' The first option is wrong because the passage says the body does defeat a new germ, only slowly; the passage never compares the safety of different vaccine types.

stem: In the passage, the phrase 'presents the immune system with' most nearly means
options: awards the immune system
explains to the immune system
performs for the immune system
offers the immune system
explanation: A vaccine 'presents the immune system with a harmless version of the germ', that is, it offers or exposes the immune system to it so the system can respond. 'Awards' suggests a prize given for merit, which does not fit, and 'explains' would require the immune system to be told something in words.

stem: According to the passage, newborn babies benefit when most people around them are immune because
options: their mothers' antibodies are made stronger by the community
a germ finds too few hosts to spread far enough to reach them
they receive memory cells from the vaccinated people around them
germs grow weaker each time they pass from one person to another
explanation: The last sentence says that when most of a community is immune, 'a germ finds too few hosts to spread, and outbreaks fade before they can reach the most vulnerable.' The passage never says memory cells pass from one person to another; each person forms their own.

title: Gutenberg's press
text: Before the middle of the fifteenth century, every book in Europe was copied by hand or printed from carved wooden blocks. A skilled scribe might need months to produce a single copy of a long work, and books were therefore rare and expensive. Around 1450, Johannes Gutenberg, working in the German city of Mainz, combined several existing technologies into a new system. Individual letters were cast in metal, arranged into lines, inked and pressed onto paper by a screw press similar to those used for making wine. Once a page had been printed, the letters could be taken apart and reused for the next one. Movable type itself was not new; printers in China and Korea had used it before him. What made Gutenberg's system so influential was the way its parts worked together, helped by Europe's alphabet of only a few dozen letters, which made casting a full set of type practical. Within fifty years, printing shops had opened in more than two hundred European towns, and millions of books had been produced. Texts that once existed in a handful of copies now circulated widely, identical from one copy to the next. Scholars in distant cities could study the same edition, compare notes and correct errors, which helped knowledge to accumulate faster than ever before.

stem: According to the passage, before about 1450 books in Europe were
options: printed with metal type brought from Korea
rare and costly, as each copy took long to make
cheap but often full of copying mistakes
made mostly in the workshops of Mainz
explanation: The passage says a scribe 'might need months to produce a single copy of a long work, and books were therefore rare and expensive.' Korea is mentioned only to show that movable type existed elsewhere, not as a source of European type.

stem: The author mentions printers in China and Korea mainly in order to
options: argue that Gutenberg copied his methods from Asian printers
explain why European books cost more than Asian ones
suggest that the alphabet was first developed in Asia
show that his real achievement was combining the parts
explanation: Right after noting that 'movable type itself was not new', the author says what made Gutenberg influential was 'the way its parts worked together'. The reference therefore shifts the credit from invention to combination. The passage makes no claim that Gutenberg copied Asian printers, so the first option goes beyond the text.

stem: As used in the final sentence, the word 'accumulate' most nearly means
options: build up
spread out
be counted
fall away
explanation: Scholars comparing notes and correcting errors made knowledge grow steadily, so 'accumulate' means build up. 'Spread out' is tempting because the passage also says texts 'circulated widely', but accumulation is about growing in amount, not moving outwards.

title: The dance of the honeybee
text: A honeybee that discovers a rich patch of flowers does not keep the news to herself. Back in the dark hive, she performs a 'waggle dance' on the vertical surface of the honeycomb. She runs a short straight line while shaking her body from side to side, then circles back to the start and repeats the run, sometimes dozens of times. In the 1940s the Austrian scientist Karl von Frisch showed that this dance is a kind of map. The angle of the straight run, measured from the vertical, matches the angle between the direction of the food and the direction of the sun. A run pointing straight up the comb means 'fly towards the sun'; a run tilted to the right means the food lies to the right of the sun. The length of each waggle run indicates distance: the longer the run lasts, the farther away the flowers are. Other bees crowd around the dancer, follow her movements and then leave to search in the direction she has shown. Von Frisch's conclusions were challenged at first, because many scientists doubted that an insect could communicate abstract information. Later experiments, including studies with robotic bees that performed the dance themselves, supported his view, and in 1973 he shared the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine.

stem: Based on the passage, a waggle run pointing straight down the comb most likely tells other bees to fly
options: directly towards the sun
only a very short distance
directly away from the sun
to the right of the sun
explanation: The angle of the run from the vertical equals the angle between the food and the sun, and straight up means 'fly towards the sun'. Straight down is 180° from straight up, so it means the opposite direction, directly away from the sun. Distance is shown by how long the run lasts, not by its direction, so 'a very short distance' does not follow.

stem: According to the passage, the length of each waggle run indicates
options: how far away the flowers are
how much nectar the flowers hold
where the sun is in the sky
how many bees should follow
explanation: The passage states: 'The length of each waggle run indicates distance: the longer the run lasts, the farther away the flowers are.' The sun's position is linked to the angle of the run, not its length.

stem: According to the passage, von Frisch's conclusions were challenged at first because many scientists
options: had watched robotic bees perform other dances
thought the dance signalled scent, not direction
found that bees ignored the position of the sun
doubted that insects could share abstract ideas
explanation: The passage says his conclusions were challenged 'because many scientists doubted that an insect could communicate abstract information.' The robotic bees came later and supported his view, so they were not a reason for doubt.

title: Nothing is truly free
text: Economists like to say that nothing is truly free. The idea behind the remark is opportunity cost: the value of the best alternative you give up when you make a choice. Suppose Sana has a free Saturday. She could work at her uncle's shop for a day's wage, revise for her examinations or spend the day with friends. If she chooses to revise, the opportunity cost of that day is not all the other options added together but only the one she would otherwise have chosen, perhaps the wage from the shop. Opportunity cost explains decisions that look puzzling at first. A free concert ticket still costs the hours spent travelling and listening, hours that could have been used for something else. A city that spends money on a new road cannot spend the same money on a hospital or a school. Even a farmer who grows wheat on his own land pays an opportunity cost, since the field could instead have grown cotton or been rented out. The concept does not tell anyone what to choose. People value things differently, and the best alternative for one person may be worthless to another. What it does is encourage a more honest comparison, reminding decision-makers to look not only at the money they spend but also at what they quietly give up.

stem: According to the passage, the opportunity cost of a choice is
options: the total value of every option not chosen
the amount of money spent on the chosen option
the value of the best alternative given up
the difference between a price and a wage
explanation: The second sentence defines opportunity cost as 'the value of the best alternative you give up when you make a choice.' The Sana example then warns that it is 'not all the other options added together', which rules out the first option.

stem: Bilal spends an evening watching a free film instead of helping at his family's bakery, which was his next best choice. According to the ideas in the passage, the opportunity cost of watching the film is
options: the help he could have given at the bakery
nothing at all, because the film was free
the price that a cinema ticket would cost
every other way he could spend the evening
explanation: Opportunity cost is the best alternative given up, and here that is helping at the bakery. The passage's free concert ticket example shows that a free event still has a cost in time, so 'nothing at all' is wrong; adding up every other option is the mistake the Sana example warns against.

stem: In the closing sentences, the author's main point is that opportunity cost
options: shows that the cheapest option is always best
proves that everyone values things alike
applies only to choices involving money
aids comparison but does not decide for us
explanation: The passage opens with 'The concept does not tell anyone what to choose' and ends by saying it 'encourage[s] a more honest comparison'. It also states that 'people value things differently', which directly contradicts the second option.

title: Mountains still rising
text: The highest mountains on Earth are, in geological terms, still being built. About fifty million years ago, the Indian plate, a vast slab of the Earth's crust that had been drifting northwards across an ancient ocean, began to collide with the Eurasian plate. Neither plate could sink easily beneath the other, because both carried thick, relatively light continental crust. Instead, the rock between them crumpled, folded and was pushed upwards, forming the Himalaya and the neighbouring Karakoram. The collision has not ended. The Indian plate continues to push north by a few centimetres a year, and parts of the Himalaya are still rising by several millimetres annually. Erosion by rivers, glaciers and landslides wears the peaks down, so their height reflects a contest between uplift from below and destruction from above. The same forces explain why northern Pakistan, India and Nepal experience frequent earthquakes. As the plates press against each other, stress builds up along cracks in the rock, called faults, until it is suddenly released. Evidence of the ancient ocean survives in surprising places: fossils of sea creatures have been found in limestone high in the mountains, thousands of metres above today's sea level.

stem: As used in the passage, the word 'contest' most nearly means
options: complaint
struggle
game
debate
explanation: The height of the peaks results from two opposing forces, 'uplift from below and destruction from above', so 'contest' means a struggle between them. 'Game' and 'debate' are kinds of contest between people and do not fit natural forces.

stem: According to the passage, the rock between the Indian and Eurasian plates was pushed upwards because
options: the Eurasian plate was moving south
the old ocean floor was very light
neither plate could easily sink below the other
glaciers had worn away the rock below
explanation: The passage states that 'neither plate could sink easily beneath the other' because both carried light continental crust, so the rock 'crumpled, folded and was pushed upwards.' It is the Indian plate that the passage says moved, northwards; nothing is said about Eurasia moving south.

stem: The discovery of fossils of sea creatures high in the mountains most directly supports which idea in the passage?
options: The mountain rock once lay beneath an ocean.
Glaciers carried sea creatures up the slopes.
Erosion is wearing the peaks down quickly.
Earthquakes are common in northern Pakistan.
explanation: The author presents the fossils as 'evidence of the ancient ocean': rock that formed under the sea was pushed up by the collision. Glaciers are mentioned only as agents of erosion that wear the peaks down, not as carriers of fossils, and the fossils say nothing about earthquakes or the speed of erosion.

title: Why cities stay hot at night
text: On a summer evening, the centre of a large city such as Lahore can be several degrees warmer than the farmland around it. This difference is known as the urban heat island effect. Its main causes lie in the materials of the city itself. Asphalt roads, concrete buildings and dark rooftops absorb sunlight during the day and release the stored heat slowly after sunset, so cities cool down far less at night than open countryside does. Air conditioners, vehicles and factories add further heat, and tall buildings packed closely together block the breezes that might carry it away. Vegetation has the opposite effect. Trees shade the ground and, through their leaves, release water vapour that cools the surrounding air as it evaporates. Areas where trees and green spaces have been replaced by pavement therefore tend to be among the hottest parts of a city. The consequences are not only uncomfortable. Hotter nights give people's bodies less chance to recover from daytime heat, which increases health risks for the elderly and for outdoor workers during heatwaves. Higher temperatures also raise the demand for electricity to run fans and air conditioners. Planting trees, protecting parks and painting roofs in light, reflective colours are among the simplest ways to reduce the effect.

stem: Which of the following best describes how the passage is organised?
options: It compares two cities and argues that one is better planned.
It tells the story of one family's experience of a heatwave.
It presents a theory and then gives evidence against it.
It names an effect, explains its causes and results, and notes remedies.
explanation: The passage names the urban heat island effect, explains its causes (materials, waste heat, blocked breezes, loss of trees), describes its consequences (health, electricity demand) and ends with simple remedies. Lahore is the only city mentioned, so there is no comparison of two cities, and no theory is disputed.

stem: According to the passage, cities cool down less at night than the countryside mainly because
options: roads and buildings release stored heat slowly
trees release water vapour into the city air
cities receive more sunlight during the day
farmland sends its heat towards the city
explanation: The passage says asphalt, concrete and dark roofs 'absorb sunlight during the day and release the stored heat slowly after sunset, so cities cool down far less at night'. Water vapour from trees cools the air, the opposite of the effect asked about.

stem: The passage suggests that painting roofs in light, reflective colours helps because such roofs
options: release water vapour that cools the air
block breezes from entering the buildings
absorb less sunlight and so store less heat
reduce the number of vehicles on the roads
explanation: Earlier the passage blames 'dark rooftops' that 'absorb sunlight during the day and release the stored heat'. A light, reflective roof does the reverse, absorbing less sunlight and so storing less heat. Releasing water vapour is how trees cool the air, not roofs.

title: Al-Khwarizmi and the method of steps
text: In the early ninth century, Baghdad was home to the House of Wisdom, a centre of learning where scholars translated Greek, Persian and Indian works into Arabic and added discoveries of their own. One of its most influential members was Muhammad ibn Musa al-Khwarizmi, a mathematician and astronomer whose family probably came from Khwarazm, a region south of the Aral Sea in Central Asia. Around 820 he wrote a book explaining how to solve practical problems of trade, inheritance and land measurement by systematic methods. Its title included the Arabic word al-jabr, meaning 'restoring', which referred to an operation for rearranging the terms of an equation. Through later Latin translations, this word gave European languages the name 'algebra'. Another of his works explained the Hindu-Arabic numerals, including a symbol for zero, and showed how calculations could be carried out with them. When this book was translated into Latin, his name was written as 'Algoritmi', the origin of the modern word 'algorithm'. What made al-Khwarizmi important was less any single result than his approach. Instead of solving each problem by a special trick, he grouped problems into types and gave step-by-step procedures that worked for every case of a type. That idea, a clear set of steps that always leads to an answer, lies at the heart of computer programming today.

stem: According to the passage, the word 'algorithm' comes from
options: the Arabic word al-jabr
the Latin form of al-Khwarizmi's name
the name of the House of Wisdom
a Persian word for calculation
explanation: The passage says that in the Latin translation 'his name was written as Algoritmi, the origin of the modern word algorithm.' Al-jabr is the source of 'algebra', not 'algorithm', which makes it the most tempting wrong choice.

stem: According to the end of the passage, al-Khwarizmi's main importance lay in
options: discovering the symbol for zero
translating Greek books into Arabic
finding a clever trick for each problem
giving general methods for types of problems
explanation: The end of the passage says he 'grouped problems into types and gave step-by-step procedures that worked for every case of a type', and that his importance lay in this approach. It explicitly contrasts this with 'solving each problem by a special trick'. The passage says he explained a symbol for zero, not that he discovered it.

stem: It can be inferred from the passage that al-Khwarizmi's ideas reached European readers mainly through
options: lectures he gave in European cities
Greek copies made in the House of Wisdom
Latin translations of his works
Indian scholars who visited Europe
explanation: Both European words linked to him arrived 'through later Latin translations': algebra from the title of one book and algorithm from the Latin form of his name in another. The House of Wisdom translated works into Arabic, not into Greek, and the passage never mentions him travelling to Europe.

title: Testing a new medicine fairly
text: When doctors test a new medicine, it is not enough to give it to sick people and see whether they get better. Many illnesses improve on their own, and patients who expect to recover often report feeling better even when they have received a pill containing nothing but sugar. This response to an inactive treatment is called the placebo effect. It is especially strong for symptoms such as pain and tiredness, which depend partly on how a person feels. To separate the real effect of a drug from these other influences, researchers use controlled trials. Volunteers are divided at random into two groups: one receives the new drug and the other a placebo that looks identical. Random division matters because it makes the groups similar in age, health and other factors, so that any difference in results can be traced to the drug. In the best trials, neither the volunteers nor the doctors treating them know who is receiving which pill until the study ends. Such a trial is called double-blind. If doctors knew, they might, without meaning to, encourage some patients more than others or judge their symptoms differently. Only when the drug group does clearly better than the placebo group do researchers conclude that the medicine works.

stem: In the passage, the phrase 'traced to' most nearly means
options: copied from
drawn around
followed towards
attributed to
explanation: Random division makes the groups alike, 'so that any difference in results can be traced to the drug', meaning the difference can be attributed to, or explained by, the drug. 'Copied from' and 'drawn around' are literal senses of trace that make no sense with results.

stem: According to the passage, volunteers are divided into groups at random so that
options: doctors can choose who receives the drug
the groups are alike except for their treatment
the placebo looks the same as the real drug
more volunteers receive the new medicine
explanation: The passage says random division 'makes the groups similar in age, health and other factors', so the treatment is the only real difference. The placebo looks identical because of how it is made, not because of the random division.

stem: The author would most likely agree that a trial in which the doctors know which patients receive the drug
options: is more reliable, as doctors can watch the drug group closely
is acceptable as long as the patients themselves do not know
may give misleading results even if the doctors are honest
cannot include a placebo group of any kind at all
explanation: The author warns that doctors who knew might, 'without meaning to', encourage some patients more or judge symptoms differently, so bias can arise without dishonesty. The second option is tempting, but the author calls trials in which neither patients nor doctors know 'the best', so hiding the facts from patients alone is not enough.

title: Galleries on wheels
text: Few sights on Pakistan's highways are as cheerful as a decorated lorry. Known around the world as truck art, the tradition turns ordinary goods vehicles into moving galleries. Every available surface is covered: painted panels show peacocks, flowers, mountain landscapes and portraits, while chains and small metal pendants hang from the bumpers and jingle as the vehicle moves. Lines of poetry or proverbs are often painted along the back. The work is done in specialist workshops in cities such as Karachi, Rawalpindi and Peshawar. A truck may spend several weeks there, passing through the hands of carpenters, metalworkers and painters, each a master of one stage. Many artists learnt the craft as apprentices, watching and assisting older painters for years before being trusted with a panel of their own. Regional styles differ, and experienced observers can often tell from the decoration where a truck was painted. For drivers who spend weeks on the road, the decoration is far more than ornament. A beautifully painted truck reflects the pride of its owner and is, in a sense, a home away from home. In recent decades the style has also moved beyond vehicles. Artists now paint furniture, kettles and shop signs in the same bright manner, and exhibitions abroad have introduced it to new audiences.

stem: The passage is mainly about
options: the dangers of driving on long highways
the history of goods transport in Pakistan
a decorative tradition and the skills behind it
the poetry written by Pakistani truck drivers
explanation: The passage describes what truck art looks like, how it is made in workshops by skilled craftsmen and what it means to drivers, then notes its spread to other objects. Poetry is mentioned only as one feature painted on trucks, and nothing says the drivers wrote it.

stem: In the passage, the word 'ornament' in 'far more than ornament' most nearly means
options: decoration
advertisement
protection
inheritance
explanation: The sentence contrasts mere decoration with the deeper meaning the painting has for drivers: pride and 'a home away from home'. 'Ornament' therefore means decoration. Nothing in the passage suggests the paintwork advertises anything or protects the vehicle.

stem: Which statement about truck art is best supported by the passage?
options: It is now made mainly for exhibitions abroad.
Each truck is decorated by one skilled painter.
Its regional styles have become almost identical.
It has personal meaning for the drivers.
explanation: The passage says a painted truck 'reflects the pride of its owner' and is 'a home away from home' for drivers. The passage says a truck passes through the hands of carpenters, metalworkers and painters, so one painter is wrong, and observers can still tell regional styles apart.

title: Water towers of ice
text: The mountains of northern Pakistan hold thousands of glaciers, among them some of the longest found anywhere outside the polar regions. Siachen, Biafo and Baltoro each stretch for more than fifty kilometres. Together these rivers of ice act as a giant water tower: snow that falls in winter is stored as ice and released as meltwater in summer, feeding the Indus and its tributaries just when farms on the plains need water most. As average temperatures rise, many glaciers in the wider Himalayan region are thinning and retreating. Melting can form lakes at a glacier's edge, held back by loose heaps of rock and ice that the glacier left behind. Such natural dams are weak. If one gives way, perhaps after a sudden ice fall or a spell of very heavy melting, the lake can empty in a few hours. The resulting rush of water, mud and boulders, known as a glacial lake outburst flood, can sweep away bridges, roads and fields far down the valley. Communities in Gilgit-Baltistan and Chitral have begun to prepare. Some valleys now have sensors that measure lake levels and early-warning systems that sound alarms, giving villagers time to move to higher ground. Mapping which lakes are growing fastest helps decide where such equipment is most needed.

stem: The author compares the glaciers to 'a giant water tower' because they
options: are taller than any building on the plains
store winter snow and release it in summer
hold back lakes behind walls of loose rock
send drinking water to cities through pipes
explanation: The comparison is explained in the same sentence: 'snow that falls in winter is stored as ice and released as meltwater in summer'. Like a water tower, the glaciers store water and release it when it is needed. Holding back lakes is done by heaps of rock and ice left by retreating glaciers, not by the glaciers acting as stores.

stem: According to the passage, the natural dams that hold back glacial lakes are weak because they
options: consist of loose rock and ice
contain old concrete that cracks
are melted by warm lake water
are cut through by rivers
explanation: The lakes are 'held back by loose heaps of rock and ice that the glacier left behind', and the next sentence calls such dams weak. The dams are natural, so concrete plays no part.

stem: It can be inferred that mapping which lakes are growing fastest is useful mainly because
options: it shows which glaciers have stopped melting
it allows the lakes to be drained more quickly
equipment can then go where the risk is greatest
it proves that average temperatures are rising
explanation: The final sentence says mapping 'helps decide where such equipment is most needed', implying sensors and alarms cannot be placed everywhere and should go to the lakes most likely to burst. The passage never mentions draining lakes, and growing lakes indicate melting, not glaciers that have stopped melting.

title: The science of dahi
text: Making dahi at home is one of the oldest uses of biotechnology. Milk is first heated, which kills most unwanted microbes, and then cooled until it is warm but not hot. A spoonful of yesterday's yogurt is stirred in, and the pot is covered and left in a warm place for several hours. By morning, the liquid milk has become a thick, slightly sour curd. The change is the work of bacteria. The starter spoonful contains lactic acid bacteria, which feed on lactose, the natural sugar in milk, and convert it into lactic acid. As acid builds up, the milk becomes more acidic, and its main proteins, which normally float freely, unfold and link together into a soft network that traps the liquid. This is why yogurt sets into a solid mass and why it tastes sour. Temperature controls the process closely. If the milk is too hot when the starter is added, the bacteria die; if it is too cold, they multiply so slowly that the milk may spoil before it sets. This explains the common household advice to wait until the milk feels comfortably warm to a fingertip. The acid also protects the yogurt, since many of the microbes that spoil food cannot grow in such sour conditions, which is why dahi keeps longer than fresh milk.

stem: According to the passage, the sour taste of yogurt comes from
options: sugar added along with the starter spoonful
proteins that unfold when milk is heated
microbes that spoil milk left overnight
acid that bacteria make from milk sugar
explanation: Lactic acid bacteria 'feed on lactose, the natural sugar in milk, and convert it into lactic acid', and the passage adds that this is 'why it tastes sour'. The proteins unfold because of the acid, not because of heating, and they explain the thickness rather than the taste.

stem: The author mentions the household advice about testing milk with a fingertip in order to
options: show that a common practice has a scientific reason
warn readers against touching milk that is boiling
suggest that thermometers give unreliable readings
explain why yogurt keeps longer than fresh milk
explanation: The advice follows the explanation that bacteria die in milk that is too hot and multiply too slowly in milk that is too cold; 'This explains the common household advice' links the practice to that science. Thermometers are never mentioned, and keeping quality is explained separately by the acid.

stem: Based on the passage, what would most likely happen if the starter were stirred into milk that was still very hot?
options: The yogurt would set faster and taste more sour.
The milk would set but taste sweeter than usual.
The milk would fail to set into yogurt.
The proteins would link together at once.
explanation: The passage states that if the milk is too hot when the starter is added, 'the bacteria die'. With no living bacteria, no lactic acid is made, so the proteins never link up and the milk does not set. The first option reverses this: heat kills the bacteria rather than speeding them up.

title: What inflation measures
text: When people say that prices have gone up, economists describe the change as inflation: a general rise in the prices of goods and services over time. Inflation does not mean that every price rises equally, or that a single item has become expensive. It means that, on average, the same amount of money buys less than it did before. If inflation is ten per cent a year, a basket of goods that cost 1,000 rupees last year costs about 1,100 rupees today. To measure inflation, statistics offices track the prices of hundreds of items that typical households buy, such as flour, cooking oil, rent, electricity and transport. Each item is weighted according to how much of a household budget it usually takes, so a rise in the price of flour counts for more than a rise in the price of ice cream. The result is a price index, whose change from one year to the next gives the inflation rate. Moderate, steady inflation is considered normal in most economies. Rapid inflation is harmful, because wages and savings often fail to keep pace. A family whose income rises by five per cent while prices rise by twelve per cent is worse off, even though it earns more rupees than before. For this reason economists often compare real incomes, which are adjusted for changes in prices.

stem: According to the passage, why does a rise in the price of flour count for more than a rise in the price of ice cream?
options: Flour is sold in far more shops than ice cream.
Flour takes a larger share of household budgets.
Ice cream prices are not tracked by the index.
Ice cream prices rise more slowly than flour.
explanation: Each item 'is weighted according to how much of a household budget it usually takes', and a typical family spends far more on flour than on ice cream. Ice cream is still in the index; its price simply carries less weight.

stem: As used in the passage, the phrase 'keep pace' most nearly means
options: rise as quickly
stay calm
walk slowly
remain unchanged
explanation: Wages and savings that 'fail to keep pace' with rapid inflation do not rise as quickly as prices, as the next sentence's example of a five per cent income rise against twelve per cent price rise shows. 'Remain unchanged' is wrong because the family's income does rise, just not fast enough.

stem: According to the reasoning of the passage, a worker whose monthly wage rises from 20,000 to 22,000 rupees in a year when prices rise by fifteen per cent
options: has a higher real income than before
has a lower real income than before
has the same real income as before
cannot be judged without her savings
explanation: The wage rises by 2,000 out of 20,000, which is ten per cent, while prices rise by fifteen per cent, so the wage buys less than before. This is the passage's five-against-twelve example in new numbers. 'Higher' is the trap: she earns more rupees, but her real income has fallen.

title: Sleeping on it
text: For much of history, sleep was regarded as little more than a pause, a time when the tired brain simply switched off. Research over recent decades has changed that picture. Sleep, it now appears, plays an active part in learning. In a typical experiment, volunteers learn a list of word pairs and are tested twelve hours later. Those who learned in the evening and slept during the interval usually remember more than those who learned in the morning and stayed awake all day, even though the same amount of time has passed. Recordings of brain activity offer a possible explanation. During deep sleep, patterns of activity linked to newly learned material seem to be replayed, and scientists believe this helps move memories from a temporary store in a structure called the hippocampus to more lasting storage in the cortex, the brain's outer layer. Sleep seems to matter before learning as well as after it. People who have been kept awake for a whole night generally find it harder to take in new information the next day, as if the temporary store had not been cleared. These findings carry a practical message for students. Staying up all night before an examination may add a few hours of reading, but it can weaken both the memory of what was studied and the ability to think clearly in the examination hall the next morning.

stem: The main purpose of the passage is to
options: describe how dreams are recorded in sleep laboratories
argue that students should study only at night
compare the sizes of the hippocampus and the cortex
explain evidence that sleep helps us learn
explanation: The passage moves from the old view of sleep as a pause to experiments and brain recordings showing that 'sleep plays an active part in learning', then draws a lesson for students. It actually warns against studying through the night, so the second option reverses its message.

stem: In the passage, the word 'regarded' in the first sentence most nearly means
options: watched
ignored
considered
respected
explanation: Sleep 'was regarded as little more than a pause' means it was considered or thought of as a pause. 'Respected' is another sense of regard, but it clashes with 'little more than', which shows a low opinion of sleep.

stem: Why does the experiment described in the passage compare volunteers who learned in the evening with those who learned in the morning?
options: to test whether people learn more easily in the evening
to keep the delay equal, so sleep is the main difference
to measure how long the hippocampus stores word pairs
to show that tired people cannot learn word pairs at all
explanation: Both groups are tested twelve hours after learning, and the passage stresses that 'the same amount of time has passed'; only the evening group sleeps in between. Equal delays leave sleep as the key difference. The study compares memory after sleep, not ease of learning at different times, so the first option misreads its design.

title: Fresh water from the sea
text: Nearly all the water on Earth is in the oceans, but it is far too salty to drink or to use on crops. Desalination plants remove the salt. The older method imitates the natural water cycle: seawater is boiled, and the steam, which leaves the salt behind, is cooled into fresh water. Boiling large volumes of water, however, takes enormous amounts of fuel. Most modern plants use reverse osmosis instead. Seawater is pumped at high pressure against a membrane whose pores are so small that water molecules can pass through but dissolved salts cannot. Fresh water collects on the other side, while a concentrated salty liquid called brine is left behind. Although reverse osmosis needs far less energy than boiling, it still requires powerful pumps, and the membranes must be cleaned or replaced regularly because algae and mineral deposits block them. For coastal cities that suffer water shortages, such as Karachi, desalination is an attractive option because the sea will never run dry. Yet it brings problems of its own. The water it produces costs more than water from rivers or wells, mainly because of the electricity used. The brine must also be disposed of carefully: released in one place, the very salty water can harm sea life near the outlet. Engineers therefore spread the discharge over a wide area or dilute it before it returns to the sea.

stem: According to the passage, the membrane used in reverse osmosis
options: lets water pass but stops dissolved salts
boils the seawater while using very little fuel
turns the leftover brine back into drinking water
never needs to be cleaned or replaced at all
explanation: The membrane's pores are 'so small that water molecules can pass through but dissolved salts cannot.' Boiling belongs to the older method, and the passage says the membranes 'must be cleaned or replaced regularly'.

stem: As used in the passage, the word 'attractive' in 'an attractive option' most nearly means
options: good-looking
appealing
colourful
magnetic
explanation: Desalination is attractive to coastal cities 'because the sea will never run dry', so the word means appealing or worth considering. 'Good-looking' is the everyday sense for people and objects, but a supply option is not being judged on its looks.

stem: According to the passage, which of the following would most directly reduce the cost of desalinated water?
options: building the plant farther from the coast
releasing all the brine at a single outlet
making the pores of the membrane smaller
cheaper electricity to run the pumps
explanation: The passage says desalinated water costs more 'mainly because of the electricity used', so cheaper electricity would cut the cost most directly. Releasing brine at one outlet is what the passage warns against, since it harms sea life near the outlet.

title: When railways set the clocks
text: Until the nineteenth century, every town kept its own time. Clocks were set by the sun, so that noon was the moment when the sun stood highest in the sky. Because the Earth turns from west to east, noon arrives earlier in eastern places than in western ones, and towns only a few dozen kilometres apart kept slightly different times. For people who travelled by horse, the difference hardly mattered. The railways changed this. A train could cross a country in hours, and its timetable had to make sense at every station. If each stop used its own local time, a schedule became confusing and, on single-track lines, even dangerous, since two trains might be sent towards each other in the belief that the line was clear. In the 1840s, British railway companies began to adopt a single standard time for all their stations, based on the clock at the Royal Observatory in Greenwich. Within a few decades most of Britain had followed. Larger countries faced a harder problem, since one time could not suit places thousands of kilometres apart. In 1884 an international conference in Washington chose Greenwich as the starting line for measuring longitude, and over the following decades most countries adopted time zones roughly fifteen degrees of longitude wide, usually one hour apart. Pakistan today uses a single zone, five hours ahead of Greenwich.

stem: Which of the following best expresses the main idea of the passage?
options: Fast rail travel made shared standard times necessary.
Noon arrives earlier in eastern towns than in western ones.
Single-track railways were the most dangerous form of travel.
The Royal Observatory at Greenwich was built for the railways.
explanation: The passage shows how local sun time worked until railways arrived, why train timetables needed a common time, and how standard time and then time zones followed. The fact about noon in eastern towns is true in the passage but is only background to that main idea.

stem: According to the passage, why could local times be dangerous on single-track lines?
options: Station clocks often stopped working when trains passed.
Drivers were unable to see the sun at noon in tunnels.
Two trains might be sent towards each other on one line.
Horses near the track were frightened by passing trains.
explanation: The passage explains that with each stop on its own time, 'two trains might be sent towards each other in the belief that the line was clear.' Horses are mentioned only as the older, slower form of travel, not as a danger on the railway.

stem: It can be inferred that, before the railways, the small differences between towns' times 'hardly mattered' because
options: every town already set its clocks by Greenwich
journeys were too slow for small gaps to matter
noon came at the same moment in every town
riders carried their own very accurate clocks
explanation: The passage contrasts horse travel with trains that 'could cross a country in hours'. On slow journeys a difference of a few minutes between towns had no practical effect. Noon did not come at the same moment everywhere; the passage says it arrives earlier in eastern places.

title: The planned city of Mohenjo-daro
text: About 4,500 years ago, on the banks of the Indus in what is now Sindh, stood one of the largest cities of the ancient world. Mohenjo-daro, as it is called today, may have housed tens of thousands of people. What most impresses visitors is not grand palaces, for none have been found, but the careful planning of ordinary life. The main streets ran roughly north to south and east to west, dividing the city into blocks. Houses were built of baked bricks of standard proportions, and many had their own bathing areas and wells. Waste water flowed from the houses into covered drains along the streets, which had openings at intervals so that they could be cleaned. On a raised mound stood the building known as the Great Bath, a large brick tank made watertight with a layer of natural tar. Its exact purpose is unknown. The people of the Indus civilisation used a script found on thousands of small seals, but no one has yet been able to read it, so much of what we know comes from buildings and objects rather than written records. Since its excavation in the 1920s, the site has suffered from salt rising through the soil and attacking the ancient bricks. It was named a World Heritage Site in 1980, and conservation work continues.

stem: According to the passage, the openings in the street drains allowed
options: rainwater to flow into the wells
the drains to be cleaned
people to bathe in the street
salt to escape from the soil
explanation: The drains 'had openings at intervals so that they could be cleaned.' Wells and bathing areas are described as features of the houses, not of the drains.

stem: According to the passage, why does much of our knowledge of Mohenjo-daro come from buildings and objects rather than written records?
options: Its people had no system of writing.
Its records were destroyed by salt.
Its seals were lost after excavation.
Its script has not yet been read.
explanation: The passage says the people 'used a script found on thousands of small seals, but no one has yet been able to read it, so' knowledge comes from buildings and objects. The first option is the trap: they did write, but their writing cannot be understood. Salt is said to damage the bricks, not records.

stem: The author's attitude towards the planning of Mohenjo-daro can best be described as
options: admiring
doubtful
indifferent
disapproving
explanation: The author says what 'most impresses visitors' is 'the careful planning of ordinary life' and goes on to describe the grid streets, standard bricks and covered drains with evident approval. Nothing in the passage questions or criticises the planning, so 'doubtful' and 'disapproving' do not fit.

title: A beautiful weed
text: Water hyacinth is a floating plant with glossy leaves and attractive lilac flowers. It is native to the Amazon basin in South America, but during the nineteenth and twentieth centuries people carried it to gardens and ponds around the world for its beauty. Escaping into rivers, lakes and canals, it has since become one of the most troublesome water weeds on several continents, including parts of South Asia. The plant's success comes from its speed. Under warm conditions it can double the area it covers in a couple of weeks, spreading both by seed and by sending out runners that grow into new plants. Outside its native range, it also lacks the insects and diseases that keep it in check at home. A thick mat of hyacinth causes many problems. It blocks sunlight from the water below, so underwater plants die, and their decay uses up oxygen that fish need. The mats clog irrigation channels and the intakes of pumps, hinder boats and fishing nets, and provide still water in which mosquitoes breed. Removing the plant by hand or machine is costly and must be repeated, because small fragments soon regrow. Some countries have had success with biological control: releasing weevils from the plant's native region that feed only on water hyacinth. Others try to make use of the harvested plant, turning it into compost, animal feed or woven baskets.

stem: In the passage, the phrase 'keep it in check' most nearly means
options: examine it closely
record its growth
keep it under control
help it to spread
explanation: Insects and diseases in the Amazon limit the plant's growth; without them elsewhere it spreads unchecked. To 'keep it in check' therefore means to keep it under control. 'Examine it closely' uses the other sense of check, as in checking work.

stem: According to the passage, a thick mat of water hyacinth harms fish mainly because
options: fish become trapped among its long roots
its flowers are poisonous to fish
weevils on it feed on fish eggs
rotting plants below it use up oxygen
explanation: The mat 'blocks sunlight from the water below, so underwater plants die, and their decay uses up oxygen that fish need.' The weevils in the passage feed only on water hyacinth, so the third option misreads them.

stem: According to the passage, water hyacinth first spread around the world because people
options: grew it in gardens for its beauty
used it as feed for their cattle
planted it to clean polluted rivers
mistook it for a useful crop
explanation: The passage says people 'carried it to gardens and ponds around the world for its beauty.' Its use as animal feed is described only at the end, as a way of using plants that have already been harvested as a weed.

title: Ibn al-Haytham and the path of light
text: How do we see? Many ancient thinkers believed that the eye sends out invisible rays that touch objects, rather as a hand feels its way in the dark. In the early eleventh century, the scholar Ibn al-Haytham, who was born in Basra and did much of his work in Cairo, set out to test such ideas by careful observation and experiment. In his Book of Optics, he argued that vision happens the other way round: light travels in straight lines from objects into the eye. He pointed out, for example, that looking at the sun hurts the eyes, which is hard to explain if the eye only sends rays out. To study how light behaves, he used a darkened room with a tiny hole in one wall. Light from the bright scene outside passed through the hole and formed an upside-down image on the opposite wall, an arrangement later known as the camera obscura. Just as important as his conclusions was his method. Ibn al-Haytham insisted that claims should be checked against controlled experiments, that measurements should be repeated, and that a scholar should examine even respected authorities critically. His book was translated into Latin and studied for centuries by European scientists, and many historians regard him as an early pioneer of the experimental approach on which modern science depends.

stem: The author mentions that looking at the sun hurts the eyes in order to
options: show that the camera obscura can damage vision
explain why the image on the wall is upside down
support the idea that light enters the eye
warn readers against repeating his experiments today
explanation: The example follows his claim that 'light travels in straight lines from objects into the eye', and the passage says the pain 'is hard to explain if the eye only sends rays out.' It is evidence for light entering the eye; the camera obscura is a separate example that comes afterwards.

stem: If a famous earlier scholar's claim disagreed with his experiments, Ibn al-Haytham, as described in the passage, would most likely have
options: accepted the claim because of the scholar's fame
trusted the results of his repeated experiments
stopped experimenting on that question
altered his measurements to match the claim
explanation: The passage says he insisted that claims be checked against controlled, repeated experiments and that 'even respected authorities' be examined critically. He would therefore trust careful evidence over reputation. Accepting the claim because of fame is exactly what his method rejects.

stem: As used in the passage, the word 'pioneer' most nearly means
options: settler
soldier
admirer
forerunner
explanation: Historians call him 'an early pioneer of the experimental approach', meaning one of the first to develop it, a forerunner. 'Settler' is the literal sense of pioneer, someone who opens up new land, which does not fit a scholar's method.

title: Sunlight on the rooftops
text: Pakistan receives strong sunshine for much of the year, and rooftop solar panels have become a common sight in its cities and villages. A solar panel is made of cells, usually of silicon, that convert light directly into electricity. When light strikes a cell, it gives energy to electrons in the silicon, and a built-in electric field pushes those electrons through a circuit as a current. There are no moving parts, which is one reason panels can last for twenty years or more. The amount of electricity a panel produces depends on more than the brightness of the sky. Panels work best when they face the sun directly, so in Pakistan, which lies north of the equator, fixed panels are usually tilted towards the south. Dust is another enemy. A layer of fine dust blocks part of the light, and in dry, dusty regions panels that are not cleaned can lose a noticeable share of their output within weeks. Surprisingly, heat is a problem too. Although panels need sunlight, their cells become less efficient as they get hotter, so a panel on a scorching June afternoon in Multan may produce less than the same panel on a bright but cool day in spring. Installers therefore leave a gap beneath the panels so that air can flow and carry heat away.

stem: According to the passage, fixed solar panels in Pakistan are usually tilted towards the south because
options: dust collects less on south-facing panels
the wind usually blows from the south
the country lies north of the equator
southern roofs stay cooler in summer
explanation: The passage says panels work best facing the sun directly, 'so in Pakistan, which lies north of the equator, fixed panels are usually tilted towards the south.' Dust is discussed as a separate problem, and nothing links it to the direction a panel faces.

stem: In the passage, the word 'enemy' in 'Dust is another enemy' most nearly means
options: source of harm
foreign army
rival in sport
personal opponent
explanation: The next sentence explains that dust 'blocks part of the light' and reduces output, so 'enemy' is used figuratively for something that does harm. Dust cannot be a personal opponent or rival, which are senses that apply only to people.

stem: Which of the following can most reasonably be inferred from the passage?
options: Panels in Multan always produce less electricity than those in cooler cities.
Panels with moving parts usually last longer than those without them.
Cleaning panels makes little difference to their output in dry regions.
Of two panels in equal sunlight, the hotter one may give less power.
explanation: The passage states that cells 'become less efficient as they get hotter', so with the same light the hotter panel can produce less. The first option is too strong: the passage compares one panel on a hot June afternoon with a cool spring day and says it 'may' produce less, not that Multan's panels always do.

title: The smallest plastic
text: Plastic does not rot in the way that wood or paper does. Instead, sunlight, waves and friction slowly break larger items, such as bags and bottles, into smaller and smaller pieces. Fragments less than five millimetres across are called microplastics. Some are made small on purpose, such as the tiny beads once common in face scrubs, and others are fibres that wash out of synthetic clothes in washing machines. Because they are so small and light, microplastics travel far. Scientists have found them in deep ocean sediments, in Arctic sea ice, in river water and in the air of cities. Sea creatures from tiny plankton to large fish swallow them, often mistaking them for food, and in this way the particles can pass along food chains. What microplastics do to living things is still being studied. In laboratory experiments, some animals that ate large amounts grew more slowly or ate less real food, because their stomachs were partly filled. The particles can also carry chemicals that stick to their surfaces. Researchers stress, however, that the effects on human health are not yet well understood. Since microplastics are almost impossible to collect once they are spread through the environment, most experts argue that the most effective response is to stop plastic waste from reaching rivers and seas in the first place.

stem: The passage is mainly concerned with
options: how plastic bags and bottles are manufactured
the nature, spread and effects of microplastics
why synthetic clothes ought to be banned worldwide
how sea ice forms in the Arctic each winter
explanation: The passage defines microplastics, traces where they travel and what they may do to living things, and ends with how best to respond. Synthetic clothes appear only as one source of fibres; the passage never argues for a ban.

stem: According to the passage, microplastics are plastic fragments that
options: float on the surface of the sea
come only from face scrubs and clothes
are less than five millimetres across
have been swallowed by sea creatures
explanation: The passage gives the definition directly: 'Fragments less than five millimetres across are called microplastics.' Face scrubs and clothes are only some of the sources; most come from larger items breaking down, so 'only' makes the second option wrong.

stem: The author's attitude towards the effects of microplastics on human health is best described as
options: cautious
alarmed
dismissive
sarcastic
explanation: The author reports that researchers 'stress' that the effects on human health 'are not yet well understood', neither raising alarm nor brushing the issue aside. 'Alarmed' is tempting because the passage describes harm to animals, but it makes no claim of harm to people.

title: Why money was invented
text: Imagine a farmer who has wheat and wants shoes. In a world without money, he must find a shoemaker who not only has shoes to spare but also happens to want wheat. Economists call this requirement a double coincidence of wants, and it makes barter, the direct exchange of goods, slow and awkward. A shoemaker who wants rice instead might refuse, and the farmer would have to arrange a chain of trades to get what he needs. Money solves this problem by acting as a medium of exchange: something everyone accepts in payment, not because they want it for itself but because they know others will accept it in turn. The farmer can sell his wheat to anyone who wants it and use the money to buy shoes from anyone who has them. Money also serves two other purposes. It is a unit of account, a common measure that lets people compare the values of very different things, from a bag of flour to a bicycle. It is also a store of value, since, unlike wheat, which may spoil, money can be saved for later use. Over history, many objects have served as money, including shells, salt, cattle and metal coins. Today most money exists only as numbers in bank records, yet it works because people trust that it will be accepted tomorrow.

stem: As used in the passage, the word 'awkward' in 'slow and awkward' most nearly means
options: shy
embarrassing
rude
inconvenient
explanation: Barter is awkward because the farmer must find a trader with exactly the right wants or arrange a chain of trades, so the word means inconvenient or difficult to manage. 'Shy' and 'embarrassing' describe awkward feelings in people, which do not fit a system of exchange.

stem: A family keeps some money in a drawer to pay school fees next year. According to the passage, this is an example of money acting as
options: a medium of exchange
a store of value
a unit of account
a coincidence of wants
explanation: The passage calls money a store of value because it 'can be saved for later use', unlike wheat, which may spoil. It becomes a medium of exchange only when it is actually spent on the fees next year.

stem: The closing sentences suggest that money works mainly because
options: it is always made of a valuable metal
banks keep a record of every coin in use
people trust others to accept it later
governments have forbidden all barter
explanation: The passage ends: money 'works because people trust that it will be accepted tomorrow', which echoes the earlier point that people accept money because 'others will accept it in turn'. Most money today exists only as numbers in bank records, so valuable metal cannot be the reason.

title: Winter haze over the plains
text: Every winter, a grey haze settles over Lahore and much of the Punjab plains, at times so thick that flights are delayed and motorways are closed. This smog is a mixture of smoke, dust and gases from many sources: vehicle exhaust, factories, brick kilns, the burning of rubbish and, in some weeks, the burning of crop stubble in fields after the rice harvest. These sources produce pollution all year round, so why is winter so much worse? Part of the answer lies in the weather. Normally, air near the ground is warmer than the air above it. Warm air rises, carrying pollutants upwards where they spread out and thin. On calm winter nights, however, the ground cools quickly, and the air touching it becomes colder than the layer above. This situation is called a temperature inversion. The warm layer acts like a lid: the cold, polluted air beneath cannot rise, and with little wind to blow it away, the pollution builds up day after day. Smog irritates the eyes and throat and can worsen asthma and other lung diseases, especially in children and the elderly. Doctors advise people to limit time outdoors on the worst days. Lasting improvement, though, depends on reducing what goes into the air: cleaner fuels and engines, modern kilns and alternatives to burning crop residue.

stem: The question in the middle of the passage mainly serves to
options: introduce the weather's role in winter smog
suggest that pollution sources disappear in summer
criticise the factories and kilns of the Punjab
move the discussion from smog to lung disease
explanation: The question is followed at once by 'Part of the answer lies in the weather' and the explanation of temperature inversions. The question itself states that the sources 'produce pollution all year round', so the second option contradicts it.

stem: According to the passage, during a temperature inversion the air near the ground is
options: warmer than the air above it
colder than the air above it
rising quickly into the sky
free of dust and smoke
explanation: On calm winter nights 'the air touching it becomes colder than the layer above. This situation is called a temperature inversion.' Warmer air near the ground is the normal situation that the inversion reverses, which makes it the tempting wrong choice.

stem: In the passage, the warm layer is said to act 'like a lid' because it
options: heats the ground during the cold night
blows the smog towards the cities
cleans pollutants out of the air
traps the polluted air beneath it
explanation: The passage explains the comparison straight away: 'the cold, polluted air beneath cannot rise', so pollution builds up as if under a lid. The passage says the ground cools quickly at night, so the warm layer does not heat it.

title: Science by volunteers
text: Science is often pictured as the work of experts in laboratories, but some of the most useful data today are collected by ordinary people. In citizen science projects, volunteers record observations that professional researchers could never gather alone. Thousands of birdwatchers count the species in their gardens on the same weekend each year; schoolchildren measure rainfall; amateur astronomers scan the night sky for new comets and exploding stars. The strength of such projects lies in numbers and spread. A single research team might survey a few sites in detail, while volunteers can cover an entire country and keep doing so year after year. Over time, their records reveal patterns, such as birds arriving earlier in spring or a butterfly spreading into new regions, that would otherwise go unnoticed. Critics once worried that data from untrained observers would be unreliable. Project designers have responded in several ways. They give clear instructions and simple identification guides, ask volunteers to upload photographs that experts can check, and use computer programs to flag records that look unusual, such as a tropical bird reported in a snowy region. Studies comparing volunteer and expert data have often found them broadly similar for common, easily recognised species, though less so for rare or confusing ones. Mobile phones have made taking part easier than ever. With a camera and an app, almost anyone can contribute to real research.

stem: Which of the following best states the main idea of the passage?
options: Well-organised volunteers can add much to scientific research.
Amateur astronomers have found more comets than professionals.
Data from untrained observers can never be trusted.
Mobile phones have replaced laboratories in modern science.
explanation: The passage explains what volunteers contribute, why their numbers and spread matter, and how careful project design makes their data reliable. The worry that untrained observers are unreliable is presented as an old criticism that designers have answered, not as the author's view.

stem: Based on the passage, volunteer records would probably be least reliable for
options: common garden birds seen every day
the amount of rain falling at a school
a rare insect resembling several others
a familiar butterfly in its usual region
explanation: Studies found volunteer and expert data broadly similar for 'common, easily recognised species, though less so for rare or confusing ones.' A rare insect that looks like several others is both rare and confusing. Common birds and a familiar butterfly fall into the reliable group.

stem: According to the passage, computer programs are used in citizen science projects to
options: identify every bird photograph automatically
point out records that look unusual
replace the work of professional experts
train new volunteers to count species
explanation: Designers 'use computer programs to flag records that look unusual, such as a tropical bird reported in a snowy region.' Photographs are checked by experts, not identified automatically by programs, so the first option misreads the passage.
